etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English worien, werien, wirien, wirwen, wyryȝen (“to choke, strangle”), from Old English wyrġan, from Proto-Germanic *wurgijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *werǵʰ- (“bind, squeeze”).

Cognate with Dutch worgen, wurgen, German würgen. Compare Latin urgere (“to press, push”), Sanskrit वृहति (vṛhati, “to tear out, pluck”), Lithuanian ver̃žti (“to string; squeeze”), Russian (poetic) отверза́ть (otverzátʹ, “to open”, literally “to untie”). Related to wring.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To be troubled; to give way to mental anxiety or doubt.
(transitive) Disturb the peace of mind of; afflict with mental agitation or distress; to exercise.

quote.citation: 2013 August 10, “Can China clean up fast enough?”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8848:
quote.text: That worries the government, which fears that environmental activism could become the foundation for more general political opposition.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To harass; to irritate or distress.
(transitive) To seize or shake by the throat, especially of a dog or wolf.

quote.citation: 1784, The House that Jack Built, page 7:
quote.text: This is the Dog, that worried the Cat, that killed the Rat, that ate the Malt, that lay in the Houſe that Jack built.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To touch repeatedly, to fiddle with.

quote.citation: 1997, David Sedaris, “A Plague of Tics”, in Naked, page 15:
quote.text: So what if I wanted to touch my nose to the windshield? Who was it hurting? Why was it that he could repeatedly worry his change and bite his lower lip without the threat of punishment?

quote.citation: 2002, Masha Hamilton, Staircase of a Thousand Steps, page 272:
quote.text: No stories, no arguments. He just worries his prayer beads.

quote.citation: 1891, “Journal of Jurisprudence and Scottish Law Magazine”, in Execution of the Judgment of Death, page 397:
quote.text: We read (Law's Memor. Pref. lix.) that "one John Brugh, a notorious warlock (wizard) in the parochin of Fossoquhy, by the space of thirty-six years, was worried at a stake and burned, 1643."

definitions.definition: An instance or cause of such a feeling.

quote.citation: 1886, Peter Christen Asbjørnsen, translated by H.L. Brækstad, Folk and Fairy Tales, page 305:
quote.text: They could never make him speak a word, although he was old enough, in short, he was a perfect worry night and day.

pronunciation: Received Pronunciation, New Zealand, General Australian
New Zealand, General Australian, UK, nonstandard
